newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia launches Supermarket to Asia plan.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia launches Supermarket to Asia plan.

text.p: Australian processed food exports to Asia are being positioned to boom under a "Supermarket to Asia" plan designed to capture a significant slice of Asia's A$83 billion food import market by year 2000.

The strategy, launched by Australian Prime Minister John Howard and the rural and retail sectors on Thursday, aims to place Australia more centrally in the total Asian food market, estimated to be worth A$685 billion by year 2000.
"This represents a significant opportunity for Australia," Howard told the Australian Food Council annual meeting in Canberra.
Chaired by Howard, a Supermarket to Asia Council was mapping out strategic growth-paths for Australian processed food through Asia's supermarket boom, speeches to the meeting said.
"The total Asian food market is estimated to be worth A$685 billion by the turn of the century, with at least 12 percent, or over A$83 billion, to be met from imports," Howard said.

The Supermarket to Asia strategy formed a key plank in the planned development of Australia's A$60 billion processed food and agriculture sector, a spokeswoman for National Farmers' Federation (NFF), a key member of the supermarket council, told Reuters. The plan was just beginning, she said.
Internationally, there had been encouraging signs of a developing solid backbone for the Supermarket to Asia strategy, Donald McGauchie, NFF president told the Food Council meeting.
A first taskforce meeting had been held in Australia to develop a White Paper on foreign policy which should recognise the strategic role of trade and the agri-business sector, McGauchie said.
The supermarket council aimed to progress sensitive issues such as quality assurance through the production and processing chain, he said.
It also would develop targeted marketing and investment strategies to take full advantage of world economic and trade opportunities, he said.

"The development of a targeted food market strategy which integrates regional and bilateral initiatives with negotiations for the next round of global trade reform (was part of a priority package)," he said.
McGauchie said reform had already begun to produce significant growth in a more Asian export-oriented food sector.
He pointed to food processing in the state of Victoria as a microcosm of Australia-wide industry trends.
Investments of A$1.2 billion had been made in food processing operations in Victoria since 1992, he said.

Food processing was now the largest single component of Victoria's manufacturing sector, at 19 percent, generating annual turnover of A$12 billion and responsible for about 35 percent of Victoria's export earnings, he said.
McGauchie listed reforms and priorities which would underpin the supermarket strategy.
"Farmers need to guarantee that the product they supply to processing companies is of the highest quality, and that they can deliver a consistent product on time every time," he said.
"Processing companies must be able to deliver the same results, and retailers must satisfy consumers on every item, every delivery, every day," he said.
Priority issues included industrial relations and the need for more flexible workplace arrangements and enhanced workplace integration, especially in the meat processing sector, he said.
There was also a need for new investment in the rural sector, with a more efficient transport chain within and between sectors was a further priority, he said.
